clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive genodermatosis caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PKP1 (plakophilin-1); the first human disease attributed to a desmosomal plaque protein.
Combines trauma-induced skin fragility with the appendage features of ectodermal dysplasia.
Painful palmoplantar keratoderma with deep fissuring is a prominent and disabling feature.
Hair is sparse and often described as astrakhan-fur-like, and the nails are dystrophic.
Perioral cracking and cheilitis are characteristic.
Electron microscopy shows small, poorly formed desmosomes with widened intercellular spaces between keratinocytes.
Failure to thrive may occur from cutaneous fluid and protein loss together with feeding difficulty.
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in PKP1, encoding plakophilin-1, an armadillo-family protein of the desmosomal plaque that clusters desmosomal cadherins and desmoplakin and anchors the keratin intermediate-filament cytoskeleton. Absence of functional plakophilin-1 impairs desmosome assembly and reduces desmosome size and number, weakening keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion; the resulting widened intercellular spaces explain the suprabasal skin fragility, while defective ectodermal appendage development produces the associated sparse hair, nail dystrophy and palmoplantar keratoderma.
additionalDifferentials: SAM syndrome (DSG1-related severe dermatitis, multiple allergies and metabolic wasting)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with light microscopy and transmission electron microscopy of desmosomes
Immunofluorescence antigen mapping demonstrating absent plakophilin-1
redFlags: Secondary cutaneous infection with risk of sepsis through eroded skin
Fluid and protein loss from extensive erosions
Disabling, painful plantar fissures limiting mobility
reference.prognosis: A chronic condition that is generally non-scarring and tends to stabilise or improve with age, though the painful keratoderma and skin fragility carry a substantial quality-of-life burden.
pitfalls: Easily misdiagnosed as epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
The painful palmoplantar keratoderma is a major morbidity that is frequently undertreated.
Should be distinguished from other desmosomal disorders such as SAM syndrome (DSG1-related).
Hair, nail and dental involvement should prompt recognition of the ectodermal dysplasia component.
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; base care on skin protection with gentle handling, emollients and prompt wound care to minimise trauma-induced erosions
Manage the painful palmoplantar keratoderma with keratolytics such as topical urea or salicylic acid, emollients, mechanical debridement and adapted footwear or orthotics
Treat and prevent secondary skin infection with antiseptics and topical or systemic antibacterials as needed
Support any hypohidrosis-related overheating with cooling measures and environmental temperature control
Provide dental care for the ectodermal appendage defects, and monitor growth and nutrition, addressing feeding difficulty and cheilitis
Coordinate multidisciplinary care led by dermatology with paediatric and dental input
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given the autosomal recessive PKP1 inheritance
